540.title: Service of the heart (Taanit 2a)
540.hook: the Talmud calls prayer the service of the heart
540.howItsDone: Jewish law asks for kavanah, focused intention, especially in the first line of the Shema and the first blessing of the Amidah, which is said quietly, lips moving, in the manner learned from Hannah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, vayifga, and the three hinges of the day: morning, afternoon, evening. Today, what prayer is, in two Hebrew words.

The Shema, said morning and evening, includes a paragraph from Deuteronomy asking people to serve God with all their heart. Serve how? You can serve with your hands: build, carry, cook, bring an offering to an altar. That's what service meant in the Temple, real physical work. But you can't hand someone your heart on a plate. The Talmud stops at that phrase and asks exactly that question.
screen: `SERVE WITH YOUR HANDS.` → `BUILD, CARRY, COOK, OFFER.` → `BUT WITH YOUR HEART?`

segments.voice: The verse is Deuteronomy eleven: "to love the LORD your God, and to serve Him with all your heart and with all your soul." At the opening of tractate Taanit, the Talmud asks: what is service that is in the heart? Its answer: this is prayer. Avodah shebalev, service of the heart. Avodah is the same word used for the priests' work in the Temple: the offerings, the incense, the daily routine. So the phrase makes a bold claim. Prayer is real service, standing alongside the Temple's. After the Temple was destroyed, that idea carried enormous weight: there was still a service anyone could bring, every day, with no altar at all. And the heart? The rabbis learned much about prayer from Hannah, at the start of the book of Samuel, praying for a child. "Now Hannah, she spoke in her heart; only her lips moved, but her voice could not be heard." From her, the Talmud learns that prayer needs the heart directed, the lips moving, and the voice kept low. Directing the heart has its own word: kavanah, intention. The siddur supplies the words; the heart does the work of meaning them. That's why it's called service. It isn't only a feeling. It's effort, like any other work.
screen: `SERVE WITH ALL YOUR HEART.` · `AVODAH: THE TEMPLE'S WORK.` · `SERVICE WITHOUT AN ALTAR.` · `HANNAH: LIPS MOVING, VOICE UNHEARD.` · then, large: `PRAYER IS THE HEART'S WORK.`

segments.voice: Let one honest sentence rise in you: thanks, a worry, a hope, a name. Say it the way Hannah did, lips moving, voice barely there, then once more, slower, meaning every word. If you pray, it can be to God in your own words; if not, say it to the quiet.
Avodah shebalev. Service of the heart. The Talmud's name for prayer.
Your line: prayer is the heart's work. The siddur gives the words, and the meaning is yours to bring. See you tomorrow.

541.title: Entering the room
541.hook: Balaam's words "how goodly are thy tents" are said on entering a synagogue
541.howItsDone: Many Jews say mah tovu (Numbers 24:5) on entering a synagogue in the morning, followed by verses from the Psalms; in many siddurim it is the first passage of the morning service.

segments.voice: Yesterday, avodah shebalev, the service of the heart. Your line was prayer is the heart's work. Today, the words many people say at the synagogue door.

Doorways change people. You lower your voice walking into a library. You straighten your back at a job interview. At some homes you take your shoes off before anyone asks. A threshold is a small border. In many synagogues, the first words people say on entering come from a surprising source: a foreign prophet who had been hired to curse.
screen: `QUIET IN THE LIBRARY.` → `SHOES OFF AT THE DOOR.` → `WORDS FROM A HIRED PROPHET.`

segments.voice: Back in Numbers, King Balak of Moab hires the prophet Balaam to curse Israel. Balaam climbs a height, looks down at the camp spread across the valley, tribe by tribe, and blessing comes out of his mouth instead: "How goodly are thy tents, O Jacob, Thy dwellings, O Israel!" In Hebrew, mah tovu: how good. What did he see? The Talmud, in Bava Batra, and Rashi after it, point to a detail. The tents were set up so that no doorway faced another. Each family had its privacy: a huge camp, and no one peering into anyone else's home. The respect was visible from the hilltop. The rabbis read tents and dwellings as houses of prayer and houses of study, so the verse became words for entering a synagogue. In many siddurim, mah tovu stands at the very beginning of the morning prayers, followed by a psalm verse about coming into God's house through God's great kindness. And there's a twist. These are an outsider's words, someone sent to do harm, who looked closely and saw goodness. A few later teachers were uneasy about opening prayer with Balaam's words. The custom stayed. Some find it moving that, in many prayer books, the morning begins with what a stranger saw: a community that respects one another's doors.

segments.voice: Picture the next doorway you'll walk through, a home, a classroom, an office, a place of worship, and see yourself stopping just before it for a single breath. If you pray, mah tovu is there: how goodly are thy tents, O Jacob. If not, notice what's good about the place you're about to enter, and the people inside.
Mah tovu. How good — Balaam's blessing on seeing Israel's tents, each respecting the other's doorway, said now on entering a synagogue.

542.title: The morning blessings
542.hook: a chain of thanks for waking: sight, clothing, standing upright
542.howItsDone: Many Jews say the morning blessings at the start of the weekday and Shabbat morning service, often led aloud by the prayer leader with the congregation answering amen, and some say them at home on waking.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mah tovu, an outsider's blessing said at the door. Your line was how good these tents. Today, the very first prayers of the morning.

Before coffee, before the phone, before anyone has said a word to you, a lot has already gone right. Your eyes opened. You could tell it was morning. You sat up, found something to wear, and your feet held you when you stood. None of it feels like news. It's the floor the day is built on, and nobody thanks a floor. The Jewish morning service thanks it anyway, one piece at a time: a short chain of blessings, each fitted to something a waking body just did.
screen: `BEFORE COFFEE, A LOT WENT RIGHT.` → `NOBODY THANKS A FLOOR.` → `A CHAIN OF THANKS.`

segments.voice: In Hebrew they're called birchot hashachar, the blessings of the dawn. Each opens with baruch atah, blessed are you, then names one gift. Who opens the eyes of the blind. Who clothes the naked. Who raises up the bowed down. Who makes firm a person's steps. The Talmud, in tractate Berakhot, page sixty b, walks through a person's waking. When you hear the rooster, say this. When you open your eyes, when you sit up, when you dress, when you stand, when your feet touch the ground, when you put on your shoes: a blessing for each motion, said at the moment it happened. So in the Talmud's telling, these blessings belong to the bedroom, not the synagogue. Over the centuries many communities moved them into the service and said them as a list. One explanation: hands weren't yet washed at the bedside, and not everyone knew the words, so the leader said them aloud and everyone answered amen. Maimonides didn't like the change; he held that each blessing belongs to its own moment. Today some people say a few at home as they wake, and many say them together in the service. Either way, the order still follows a body getting up. Underneath is a simple rule: the Talmud teaches that a person shouldn't enjoy anything in this world without a blessing, and waking up is the first thing you enjoy. Sight and steady legs aren't small just because they're common.

segments.voice: Start with the breath, going in and out without being asked, then pick two more things your body does: your eyes taking in the room, your hands, your heartbeat. Stay a few breaths with each and notice it working. If you pray, begin each with baruch atah, blessed are you; if not, a plain thank you is enough.
Birchot hashachar. The blessings of the dawn: a chain of short thanks for waking, seeing, dressing and standing.
Your line: thanks for the basics. Nobody thanks a floor, but this chain of blessings does. Until tomorrow.

543.title: The rooster's understanding
543.hook: the first morning blessing thanks God for giving the rooster sense to tell day from night
543.howItsDone: The blessing over the rooster is the first of the morning blessings in many Jewish prayer books; the Talmud ties it to hearing the rooster at dawn, and today it is said at home on waking or at the start of the morning service.

segments.voice: Yesterday, birchot hashachar, the chain of blessings for a waking body. Your line was thanks for the basics. Today, the first link in the chain.

A town in the days of the Talmud. No alarm clock, no streetlights, no glowing phone. Just dark, then less dark, and before the sun is up, a rooster. The baker hears it and gets up for the dough. The shepherd reaches for his cloak. That cry was the town's clock. And when the prayer book lines up its dawn blessings, the first link isn't about you at all. It's about the bird outside the window.
screen: `NO ALARM CLOCK.` → `THE ROOSTER WAS THE TOWN'S CLOCK.` → `THE FIRST LINK IS ABOUT A BIRD.`

segments.voice: The blessing says: blessed are you, who gave the sechvi understanding to tell day from night. The Talmud, in Berakhot, page sixty b, says to say it when you hear the rooster call. And sechvi is a puzzle. In the Bible it turns up in the Book of Job, where God asks who gave understanding to the sechvi. Translators don't agree what it means there; some read it as the mind or the heart, and the 1917 Jewish translation chose mind. But the Talmud, in tractate Rosh Hashanah, reports that in one region people called a rooster a sechvi. So the rabbis heard Job's question as: who taught the rooster to know when morning comes? Later commentators kept both meanings at once. The rooster knows night from day, and so does the human heart, if it's paying attention. The blessing thanks God for the bird, and for the mind that hears it. This understanding isn't cleverness, or knowing facts. It's binah, discernment: telling one thing from another. It echoes the first day of creation, when God divides the light from the darkness. In this prayer book, the day begins with a distinction. It's morning now. Night is over. Whatever happened in the dark doesn't have to set the tone for the light.
screen: `WHO GAVE THE SECHVI UNDERSTANDING?` · `A WORD FROM THE BOOK OF JOB.` · `THE ROOSTER, AND THE HEART.` · `BINAH: TELLING ONE THING FROM ANOTHER.` · then, large: `TELL DAY FROM NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and let your ears go out past the edges of the room: traffic, a bird, a neighbor's door, the hum of a fridge. Wait for one sound that tells you something about this hour, and stay with it; let it be your rooster. Notice that you knew what it meant without thinking.
Sechvi. Read by the Talmud as rooster, the first morning blessing thanks God for the creature, and the mind, that can tell day from night.
Your line: tell day from night. Whatever happened in the dark, the morning gets its own start. Day five hundred forty-three, done.

544.title: Opening blind eyes
544.hook: blessings for sight, freedom, clothing and steady steps
544.howItsDone: These blessings are part of the morning blessings said at home on waking or at the start of the morning service, and in many synagogues the leader chants them aloud while the congregation answers amen.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sechvi, the rooster's understanding, the first blessing of the morning. Your line was tell day from night. Today, the eyes open.

Your eyes open in the morning and the room comes back: ceiling, curtain, the chair with yesterday's clothes on it. It takes half a second, and you've done it every day of your life. The prayer book doesn't call that half second waking up. It calls it opening the eyes of the blind. And it keeps going in that key. Sitting up becomes setting the captive free. Getting dressed becomes clothing the naked. Big words, the words of rescue, for the smallest motions of a morning.
screen: `THE ROOM COMES BACK.` → `OPENING THE EYES OF THE BLIND.` → `BIG WORDS FOR SMALL MOTIONS.`

segments.voice: The Talmud, in Berakhot, pairs each blessing with a motion. When you open your eyes: blessed are you, pokeach ivrim, who opens the eyes of the blind. When you sit up and stretch: matir asurim, who frees the bound, because a body stiff from sleep has just been let loose. When you dress: malbish arumim, who clothes the naked. When you stand up straight: zokef kefufim, who raises the bowed down. When you start to walk: who makes firm a person's steps. Several of these phrases are lifted almost word for word from the Psalms. Psalm one hundred forty-six, in the old Jewish translation, says: "The LORD looseth the prisoners; the LORD openeth the eyes of the blind; the LORD raiseth up them that are bowed down." In the psalm, those are rescues: God lifting the people who have the least. The prayer book borrows that language for your ordinary morning. Why? The Talmud elsewhere calls sleep a sixtieth part of death. Seen that way, every waking is a small return, from not seeing to seeing, from lying still to moving. Many people hear a second layer too. To say who opens the eyes of the blind is to remember that for some people sight is not a given, and freedom isn't, and clothing isn't. The blessing thanks God for your morning in words that keep other people's mornings in view.

segments.voice: Close your eyes for a few breaths, then open them slowly, as if for the first time today, and let your gaze land on one thing: a cup, a plant, a patch of light, your own hand. Look longer than you normally would, at its color, its edges, its shadow. If you pray, you can say pokeach ivrim; if not, just keep looking.
Pokeach ivrim. Who opens the eyes of the blind — the morning blessing for sight, borrowed word for word from a psalm about rescue.
Your line: eyes opened. The smallest motions of a morning get the words of rescue. See you tomorrow.

545.title: Strength to the weary
545.hook: a later blessing thanks God for giving strength to the tired
545.tomorrow: The soul you gave me is pure
545.howItsDone: Many Jewish prayer books include the blessing 'who gives strength to the weary' among the morning blessings, often as the last of the series, said at home or at the start of the morning service.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pokeach ivrim, blessings for sight, freedom and clothing, borrowed from a psalm. Your line was eyes opened. Today, a blessing for people who wake up tired.

Not everybody wakes up rested. The baby was up at three. The worry was up at four. Some mornings the first thing you feel is how heavy your arms are. A prayer book that only thanked God for bright, bouncing mornings would leave a lot of people out. So near the end of the morning blessings, many prayer books carry one that seems written for exactly this person. It isn't in the Talmud's list. It came later, and it stuck.
screen: `NOT EVERYBODY WAKES UP RESTED.` → `THE BABY AT THREE.` → `A BLESSING THAT CAME LATER.`

segments.voice: The words are: blessed are you, hanoten laya'ef koach, who gives strength to the weary. The phrase comes from Isaiah, chapter forty, in the old Jewish translation: "He giveth power to the faint." A few verses on, Isaiah promises that those who wait for God will renew their strength, and run, and not be weary. Ya'ef means worn out from effort, the tiredness of someone who has been working or walking a long way. The Talmud's list of waking blessings doesn't include this one. It shows up in the medieval prayer books of France and Germany, and spread from there. Some authorities hesitated: Rabbi Joseph Karo, author of the Shulchan Aruch, the code of Jewish law, was uneasy about a blessing the Talmud never mentions. But the custom held, and today it's widely said, in many communities as the last of the morning blessings. Look where it lands. After the blessings for eyes and legs and clothes, one more line admits something honest: you're up, but you may not be full of energy. It doesn't say who makes the weary cheerful. It says who gives them strength, enough to begin. Sleep is treated as a gift that restores, and the morning thanks God for what was restored, even if only partly.
screen: `HANOTEN LAYA'EF KOACH.` · `FROM ISAIAH 40.` · `NOT IN THE TALMUD'S LIST.` · `ENOUGH STRENGTH TO BEGIN.` · then, large: `STRENGTH TO THE WEARY.`

segments.voice: Let your shoulders drop and your hands go heavy, and admit how tired you actually are right now, on a scale of one to ten. Then breathe slowly and feel what's still there under the tiredness: a heartbeat, a breath, enough strength to sit here. If you pray, you can say hanoten laya'ef koach.
Ya'ef. Worn out from effort — the later morning blessing hanoten laya'ef koach gives strength to everyone who wakes up tired, even partly restored.
Your line: enough to begin. Not cheerful, not full of energy, just strong enough to start. That's day five hundred forty-five.

546.title: The soul you gave me is pure
546.hook: Elohai Neshamah: my God, the soul you placed in me is pure
546.howItsDone: Elohai neshamah is said each morning among the morning blessings, at home or in the synagogue; many people also say the short Modeh Ani on first waking and Elohai neshamah after washing their hands.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a later blessing for people who wake up tired. Your line was enough to begin. Today, the blessing for the soul.

What's the first thing your mind says to you in the morning? For some people it's a list of failures. You didn't finish that. You said the wrong thing. You're behind. The inner critic is awake first. Now set beside that the line the Talmud says to say on waking, before the blessings for eyes and legs and clothes. It doesn't begin with what you did wrong, or what you owe. It begins with one word about who you are: pure.
screen: `THE INNER CRITIC WAKES FIRST.` → `A DIFFERENT FIRST WORD.` → `PURE.`

segments.voice: The prayer is called Elohai neshamah, my God, the soul. In the Talmud, in Berakhot, it runs roughly like this: my God, the soul you placed in me is pure. You created it, you formed it, you breathed it into me. You guard it within me, and one day you will take it from me, and return it in the time to come. As long as the soul is in me, I give thanks. And it ends: blessed are you, who restores souls to bodies. Neshamah means soul, and it's close kin to the Hebrew word for breath. In Genesis, the old Jewish translation says God "breathed into his nostrils the breath of life." Breath of life there is nishmat chayim. So you breathed it into me points back to the first human, and to every breath since. Notice the order. Before thanks, before requests, before any confession, the prayer states: the soul is pure. Jewish teachers point to this line to say that each morning a person starts with a clean soul. Mistakes are real, and the tradition takes repair very seriously. But the soul itself isn't the mistake. The prayer is honest about death too: one day the soul will be taken. That's why waking is treated as a return. In the prayer's telling, it was given back again this morning.
screen: `ELOHAI NESHAMAH: MY GOD, THE SOUL.` · `NESHAMAH: SOUL, AND BREATH.` · `PURE, BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE.` · `WAKING IS A RETURN.` · then, large: `THE SOUL IS PURE.`

segments.voice: Feel the air come in through your nose, cool, and go out, warm. Breathing in, think neshamah, breath and soul together; breathing out, say pure, aloud or inside. If the critic starts its list, let it talk, and keep breathing under it.
Neshamah. Soul, close kin to the word for breath: the soul the morning prayer calls pure.
Your line: the soul is pure. A week of the heart's work, the doorway, the dawn blessings, the rooster, opened eyes, strength for the weary, and a pure soul. Rest well.
